item.title: US Department of Labor awards $81.5M in grants to support industry-driven job training programs in rural communities
item.description: WASHINGTON – The U.S. Department of Labor today announced the award of $81.5 million in funding to address the critical workforce needs of employers in high-growth and emerging industries across the Appalachian, Delta, and Northern Border regions. item.title: US Department of Labor awards more than $10.5M in grants to support mine safety, health training across the nation
item.description: WASHINGTON – The U.S. Department of Labor announced today that its Mine Safety and Health Administration has awarded more than $10.5 million in grants to reduce mining accidents, injuries, and illnesses by supporting training and education programs.The agency is awarding these grants to support the delivery of federally mandated training for new and experienced miners at surface and underground coal and metal and nonmetal mines. MSHA is awarding grants in 45 states, the Navajo Nation, and the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands.“Thanks to President Trump’s leadership we’re investing billions of dollars into critical mining projects and resources for mining education,” said Secretary of Labor Keith Sonderling. “Today’s grant announcement furthers the Department’s goal to expand mining across the United States to support this Administration’s goals to provide critical resources to the workers industries that continue to expand in America.”States and territories apply for grant funding, which is then awarded to state mine inspectors’ offices, state departments of labor, and state-supported colleges and universities. Training and education programs are tailored locally to address conditions and hazards miners may experience.“A strong and thriving America relies on a mining industry that safely produces the minerals essential to our economy,” said Assistant Secretary for Mine Safety and Health Wayne Palmer. “These grants will promote safe and healthful workplaces for over 300,000 miners across 47 states, territories, and tribal lands.”Learn more about MSHA.The recipients of MSHA State Grants are as follows: RecipientCityState/TerritoryAwardBevill State Community College JasperAL $243,711University of Alaska at FairbanksFairbanksAK $160,886Arizona State Mine Inspector’s OfficePhoenixAZ $453,633Navajo Nation Minerals DepartmentWindow RockAZ $46,430Arkansas Department of Labor and LicensingLittle Rock AR $138,903Central Connecticut State UniversityNew BritainCT $98

item.title: Hours of Service of Drivers: Association of American Railroads and American Short Line and Regional Railroad Association; Application for Exemption Renewal
item.description: FMCSA announces its final decision to renew and modify the exemption granted to the Association of American Railroads and the American Short Line and Regional Railroad Association and member railroads (the Associations) from the hours-of-service (HOS) prohibitions against driving after the 14th hour after coming on duty (the 14-hour rule) and against driving after accumulating 60 hours of on duty time within 7 consecutive days, or 70 hours of on duty time within 8 consecutive days (the 60-hour/70-hour rule). The exemption will enable covered drivers to respond to unplanned events that occur outside of, or extend beyond, their normal work hours. FMCSA modifies the previous exemption to limit the categories of unplanned events during which the exemption may be used and to add reporting requirements. In addition, only drivers operating for motor carriers listed in the Appendix to this decision may operate under the exemption. FMCSA has analyzed the exemption application and has determined that the exemption renewal, subject to the terms and conditions set forth below, is likely to achieve a level of safety that is equivalent to or greater than the level that would be achieved in the absence of the exemption.

item.title: US Department of Labor secures court order requiring New Jersey employer to pay $700K in back wages, damages to 48 workers denied overtime pay
item.description: VOORHEES, NJ – The U.S. Department of Labor has obtained a consent judgment and final order in federal district court requiring a New Jersey drywall installer to pay $725,000 in back wages, damages, and civil money penalties after denying 48 workers overtime pay.The department’s Wage and Hour Division found that P & B Partitions Inc. failed to pay their employees for pre-shift work while they waited for transportation to their jobsites. The failure to pay constitutes a violation under the Fair Labor Standards Act’s overtime provisions. “Tasks completed to prepare for the job, and in this case, while waiting to get to the worksite, is work that must be compensated,” said Wage and Hour Division District Director Charlene Rachor in Southern New Jersey. “Failing to pay workers overtime wages deprives them of their rights, and we will hold employers accountable for such actions.”The consent judgment requires P & B Partitions Inc. to pay $350,000 in back wages, an equal amount in liquidated damages to 48 workers, and requires payment of an additional $25,000 in civil penalties. The judgment was entered in the U.S. District Court for the District of New Jersey on June 26, 2026.“The U.S. Department of Labor will pursue legal action to ensure that all employees receive the compensation they are legally owed,” said Regional Solicitor of Labor Jeffrey S. The failure to pay constitutes a violation under the Fair Labor Standards Act’s overtime provisions. “Tasks completed to prepare for the job, and in this case, while waiting to get to the worksite, is work that must be compensated,” said Wage and Hour Division District Director Charlene Rachor in Southern New Jersey. “Failing to pay workers overtime wages deprives them of their rights, and we will hold employers accountable for such actions.”The consent judgment requires P & B Partitions Inc. to pay $350,000 in back wages, an equal amount in liquidated damages to 48 workers, and requires payment of an additional $25,000 in civil penalties. The judgment was entered in the U.S. District Court for the District of New Jersey on June 26, 2026.“The U.S. Department of Labor will pursue legal action to ensure that all employees receive the compensation they are legally owed,” said Regional Solicitor of Labor Jeffrey S. Rogoff in New York. “This case demonstrates that employers can face costly consequences if they do not comply with federal wage law.”Employees and employers can contact the Wage and Hour Division with questions and requests for compliance assistance at its toll-free helpline, 866-4US-WAGE (487-9243). Employers are encouraged to use the agency’s industry-specific compliance assistance toolkits to learn about their responsibilities under the laws enforced by the division. item.title: US Department of Labor obtains consent order against retirement plan fiduciaries of defunct Chicago law firm for failing to distribute $6.4M in assets
item.description: CHICAGO – Following a complaint filed by the U.S. Department of Labor, a defunct Chicago law firm’s retirement plan distributed $6,498,858 in retirement plan assets to 40 employees. The plan’s fiduciaries failed to properly terminate the plan and disburse those funds as required by law.On Aug. 18, 2026, the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Illinois, Eastern Division, entered a consent order resolving the department’s claims against the McCullough, Campbell & Lane LLP, and the firm’s capital partners David L. Joslyn, John W. McCullough, F. Dennis Nelson, and Paul S. Turner. The department alleged that the defendants violated the Employee Retirement Income Security Act by failing to follow a 2019 partnership resolution. The resolution required them to terminate the firm’s retirement plan and distribute the plan’s assets to employees. The defendants have provided proof that plan’s assets were distributed to participants, except for approximately $13,861 in the employer-level plan accounts. The consent order requires the plan’s recordkeeper to distribute those funds to its participants and to terminate the plan. “After their law firm closed, Turner, McCullough, Nelson, and Joslyn failed to provide employees with their promised retirement benefits,” said Employee Benefits Security Administration Regional Director Kelli Hammerl in Chicago. “The Department of Labor helped participants gain access to their retirement savings.” The order permanently bars Turner, McCullough, Nelson, and Joslyn from serving as fiduciaries or service providers for any ERISA-covered employee benefit plan. Judicial Branch Ends Attorney Entry Screening Bypass Program and Announces Procedure for Reimbursement

Date: 11/17/2026

Beginning January 1, 2027, attorneys entering state courthouses will no longer be able to bypass security screening. Attorneys who show their bar cards (which can be downloaded from the Board of Bar Overseers website) will be able to go to the head of the screening line. In some courthouses, there may be a separate "attorneys only" line if resources allow.

Chief Justice Stanfill spoke to the policy change: The Judicial Branch continuously reviews our security protocols to ensure appropriate measures are in place. We believe this policy change provides greater protection for all people using the courthouse. The policy change follows best practices for courthouse security and aligns with the policy of the federal courts in Maine and the state courts of most other New England states.

The Judicial Branch stopped issuing security cards to attorneys in May 2026. Attorneys whose security cards have not expired by January 1, 2027, will be able to receive a pro rata refund of the fee for the unexpired portion. Instructions and the form for requesting a refund are posted on the For Attorneys page of the Judicial Branch website and can be downloaded directly here: https://www.courts.maine.gov/attorneys/atty-security-card-reimbursement.pdf

The proposed rule modernizes the Permanent Labor Certification program by strengthening recruitment standards and recordkeeping requirements, eliminating administrative exemptions to the statutory labor market test, and improving safeguards for all American workers, especially those affected by layoffs. This proposed update to the PERM program – the first comprehensive set of regulatory reforms to the program in nearly 20 years – will ensure that highly qualified American workers receive fair consideration and first access to job opportunities.“American Workers are the best in the world, and they deserve the first and best job opportunities. Existing regulations have instead allowed companies to sponsor foreign workers without fully considering American workers first,” said Secretary of Labor Keith Sonderling. “This proposed rule change will ensure American workers are first in line for high-skilled, high-paying job opportunities over foreign labor.”The proposed rule would require employers to level the playing field when recruiting workers by using the same channels and methods when advertising jobs. Proposed changes include a requirement to replace print-based job advertisements with online recruiting through employer websites, online job boards, social media, job fairs, and campus recruitment. Employers would also be required to advertise positions for at least 90 calendar days and demonstrate that they made good-faith efforts to recruit qualified American workers. Under the proposal, employers would be prohibited from tailoring job opportunities to foreign workers. The department also proposed to eliminate the administrative exemption employers used to bypass the statutory labor market test for certain occupations. Under the proposal, employers recruiting for physical therapists, nurses, and workers with exceptional abilities in the sciences or arts would be required to consider qualified U.S. workers. The proposed rule also protects qualified American workers affected by layoffs by requiring ongoing consideration of laid off workers throughout the labor certification and immigrant petition processes, and prohibiting certain employers that have laid off American workers within the last 2 years from seeking permanent labor certification for the same or similar positions. Comments on the proposed rule are due 60 days after publication in the Federal Register. Additional information is available on ETA’s Office of Foreign Labor Certification website.

The proposal gives fiduciaries an affirmative expression of their duty of loyalty, which would clarify that ERISA requires plan fiduciaries to act solely in the interest of the plan’s participants and beneficiaries, and for the exclusive purpose of providing for the interests of participants and beneficiaries in their retirement income or financial benefits under the plan.“President Trump’s Department of Labor is not putting its thumb on the scale for or against any particular investment or asset class,” said U.S. Secretary of Labor Keith Sonderling. “Our proposed rule makes clear that retirement plan fiduciaries must make investment decisions solely in the financial interests of workers and retirees, not to advance political or social agendas. Our focus is on protecting and growing Americans’ retirement savings, which have reached record levels thanks to President Trump.”If finalized, the proposal would also place a heightened focus on shareholder engagement and proxy voting by fiduciaries to secure the retirement interests of American workers and would avoid the improper pressures and influence placed on plan fiduciaries. This includes voting shares and otherwise attempting to influence corporate behavior through shareholder engagement activities for ESG/DEI purposes. The proposed rule follows the directive in President Trump’s executive order, “Protecting American Investors from Foreign-Owned and Politically Motivated Proxy Advisors,” which instructed the department to strengthen the fiduciary standards of pension and retirement plans covered by ERISA.“President Trump has directed the department to assess whether certain proxy advisor firms spreading ESG and DEI are acting solely in the financial interest of plan participants,” said Assistant Secretary for the Employee Benefits Security Administration Daniel Aronowitz. “Our proposed rule does just that by making clear what is, and what isn’t, loyal behavior when it comes to proxy voting and shareholder engagement.” The proposal would remove two departmental inventions that are not consistent with ERISA and may be misused by fiduciaries with ulterior motives – the tiebreaker test and the participant preference provision. Under the tiebreaker test, a fiduciary can say that two investments are “equal” and then pick their preferred investment, which may include ESG funds. Similarly, fiduciaries can elicit the views of participants who support ESG investments and use that as a pretext to permit investments they otherwise would not be allowed to include under federal retirement laws. The proposed rule will be published in the Nov. 24 edition of the Federal Register, with public comments due 60 days after its publication.EBSA ensures the security of retirement, health, and other job-based benefits for American workers and their families. The agency is responsible for protecting more than 155 million workers, retirees, and their families, who are covered by approximately 2.8 million health plans, 837,000 private retirement plans, and 521,000 additional welfare benefit plans. Together, these plans hold about $15.2 trillion in assets.Employers and workers can contact EBSA at askebsa.dol.gov or call 866-444-3272 toll-free for help with private sector job-based retirement and health plans.Read the notice of proposed rulemaking on Loyalty and the Exclusive Purpose Rule in Selecting Plan Investments and Exercising Shareholder Rights.
